title.en: The Eldest Magician: Earth of a Tray, Heaven of an Umbrella
title.zh: 太初魔法師：盤大之地，傘大之天

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (collected from charm-books and magicians)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（採自符咒書與巫師）

texts.period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I 'Nature', the cosmogonic excerpts from Malay charm-books

summary.en: A Malay charm-book opens creation with the Eldest Magician: before the spheres existed, the Creator pre-existed by Himself and made the Earth 'of the width of a tray and the Heavens of the width of an umbrella.' In a second charm the word Kun ('Be!') is spoken by God and echoed by Muhammad; the seed becomes a root, the root a tree, the tree brings forth leaves, and heaven and earth take shape around it.
summary.zh: 馬來符咒書以『太初魔法師』開篇：混沌未分，造物主獨存，先造『盤大之地』與『傘大之天』。另一咒云：神言『昆』（Kun，即是！），穆罕默德應之；種子生根、根成樹、樹生葉，天地遂成。

sensitivity.note: Malay Islamic-folk cosmogony recorded from magicians' charm-books; a syncretism of Qur'anic 'Kun' with older Malay imagery, noted by Skeat himself.

passages.text: Before the spheres, or of Space and Void, the Creator of the entire Universe pre-existed by Himself, and He was the Eldest Magician. He created the Earth of the width of a tray and the Heavens of the width of an umbrella, which are the universe of the Magician. From before the beginning of time existed that Magician — that is, God — and He made Himself manifest with the brightness of the moon and the sun, which is the token of the True Magician.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: In another charm, 'Kun' said God, 'Payah kun' said Muhammad, and a seed was created. The seed became a root, the root a tree, and the tree brought forth leaves. Then Heaven and Earth were created — Earth of the width of a tray, Heaven of the width of an umbrella.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: The Navel of the Earth: A Tree of Four Branches

region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（符咒書宇宙觀）

texts.period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, the pillar of the Ka'bah as Navel of the Earth

summary.en: God 'created the pillar of the Ka'bah, which is the Navel of the Earth, whose growth is comparable to a Tree, whose branches are four in number' — Sajeratul Mentahar, Taubi, Khaldi, and Nasrun 'Alam — extending north, south, east and west, 'where they are called the Four Corners of the World.' A Malay charm-book thus fuses the world-axis and the world-tree under the navel-stone of Mecca.
summary.zh: 神『造克爾白之柱，即大地之臍，其生長如樹，樹有四枝』——薩傑拉圖勒·門塔哈爾、陶比、哈爾迪、納斯倫·阿拉姆——分向東西南北延伸，『是為世界四隅』。馬來符咒書以麥加之臍石統合世界軸與世界樹。

sensitivity.note: Syncretic world-tree; treated respectfully as recorded folk cosmology.

passages.text: The account proceeds to describe how God 'created the pillar of the Ka'bah, which is the Navel of the Earth, whose growth is comparable to a Tree, whose branches are four in number, and are called, the first Sajeratul Mentahar, and the second Taubi, and the third Khaldi, and the fourth Nasrun 'Alam, which extend unto the north, south, east, and west, where they are called the Four Corners of the World.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: The Serpent Broken in Two: How Sakatimuna's Body Made the World
title.zh: 巨蛇斷為兩截：薩卡蒂穆納之軀化成世界

region.en: Menangcabow, Sumatra (origin of the serpent myth), recorded in Selangor charm-books
region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保（蛇神話之源），雪蘭莪符咒書採錄

texts.period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, Gabriel kills the serpent Sakatimuna

summary.en: God's word comes in secret to Gabriel: 'Take me down the iron staff of the Creed which dangles at the gate of heaven, and kill me this serpent Sakatimuna.' Gabriel does so; the serpent breaks asunder, its head shooting above the heavens, its tail penetrating beneath the earth — and its body becomes the world: the rainbow from its sword, grass from the hair of its body, trees from the hair of its head, rain from its tears, dew from its sweat, and genii of every kind from its remains.
summary.zh: 神諭密告迦伯列：『取下懸於天門之鐵杖，為我誅殺巨蛇薩卡蒂穆納。』迦伯列從命；蛇身斷裂——首部直上諸天，尾部下穿大地——其軀化成萬象：虹霓出自其劍，草出自身毛，樹出自頭髮，雨出自其淚，露出自其汗，精怪自其餘軀而生。

sensitivity.note: Dismembered-primordial-being cluster (compare Purusha, Ymir, Pangu, Tiamat); Skeat notes the anthropomorphic serpent as likely an Indian Naga reminiscence — flagged as interpretive. Cross-cluster: the same serpent-name Sakatimuna appears slain by Sang Sapurba in the Malay Annals.

narrative.en:
Among the cosmogonic excerpts that Skeat collected from Malay charm-books and magicians in Selangor, the most dramatic is the killing of the primordial serpent Sakatimuna — a serpent remembered (Skeat notes, citing Newbold and Leyden) as having ravaged the country of Menangkabau in Sumatra about the twelfth century, and the same monster-name that the Malay Annals gives as slain by Sang Sapurba's champion.

BEGINNING: THE COMMISSION. God's word comes in secret to Gabriel: 'Take me down the iron staff of the 'Creed' which dangles at the gate of heaven, and kill me this serpent Sakatimuna.' The weapon is itself sacred — a staff inscribed with the confession of faith, hanging at heaven's gate; the snake must be killed from above.

MIDDLE: THE BREAKING. Gabriel does as commanded, and the serpent 'brake asunder, the head and forepart shooting up above the heavens, and the tail part penetrating downwards beneath the earth.' The world is thus split open at the moment of the serpent's death: a being who spanned both heaven and earth is cut at the middle, and its two halves become the bounds of the upper and lower worlds.

END: THE ANATOMY OF THE WORLD. The rest of the charm describes the transformation of the serpent's parts into the things of the world — 'the rainbow from the serpent's sword with its hilt and cross-piece, grass from the hair of its body, trees from the hair of its head, rain from its tears, and dew from its sweat,' while most of its anatomy turns into the good and evil genii that crowd Malay popular belief. Skeat draws out the remarkable anthropomorphism: this is 'a serpent in little more than name,' likely a reminiscence of the Indian Naga — and he compares the seated human figure with folded arms on every Malay kris hilt.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) explains natural phenomena (rain, dew, grass, trees, the rainbow) from a slain primordial body; (2) fixes the vertical axis of the Malay cosmos (head above heaven, tail below earth); (3) peoples the spirit-world (genii from the serpent's remains); and (4) links the Malay folk cosmology to the historical dragon-slayer tradition of Menangcabow (Sang Sapurba in the Annals, with the sword of one hundred and ninety notches in the Sultan of Pagaruyung's title-list) — the same monster, slain twice: once at creation, once at the founding of kingship. The charm's geography deserves a final note: because the serpent's head shoots above the heavens and its tail below the earth, the Malay world inherits a vertical ladder along which prayer, smoke and spirit-travel all move — the same axis the Kayan tree-ladder and the Ka'bah-as-navel-tree express in their own idioms. The serpent's notional death also explains why the genii born from its remains are ambivalent: they are the leftovers of a primordial killing, neither wholly good nor wholly bad, and the charm-books' invocations address them as kin rather than strangers. The Menangcabow connection closes the loop in time as well as space: a serpent that ravaged the highlands in the twelfth century, was slain by a champion whose sword still shows the notches, and was killed once more at the beginning of the world in the charm-books' memory — the same monster met twice, once by kings and once by creation.
narrative.zh: 斯凱特在雪蘭莪所採之馬來符咒書宇宙論中，最戲劇者為誅殺原初巨蛇薩卡蒂穆納——此蛇名亦見於《馬來紀年》（蘇門答臘米南加保十二世紀之害獸；三蘇爾巴勇士所誅者同名）。神諭密告迦伯列執天門之鐵杖（刻有信仰箴言）誅蛇；蛇斷為兩截——首上諸天，尾下穿地——世界於蛇死之刻被劈開。蛇軀化成萬象：虹出自劍、草出身毛、樹出頭髮、雨出淚、露出汗；其餘遺骸化為善惡精怪。斯凱特指出其強烈擬人特徵，謂近似印度那伽。功能：釋自然現象、立宇宙縱軸、生精怪世界、並與米南加保屠龍王權傳統（紀年中三蘇爾巴誅蛇、巴加爾容王列劍一百九十缺口）相銜——同一怪物，死於創世，又死於王權之始。

functions: Explains rain, dew, grass, trees and the rainbow as transformations of a slain primordial serpent
Fixes the vertical axis of the Malay cosmos: serpent head above heaven, tail beneath the earth
Peoples the Malay spirit-world: good and evil genii born from the serpent's remains
Links folk cosmology to the Minangkabau dragon-slayer kingship tradition (Sacatimuna of the Malay Annals)

variants.name: Sakatimuna/Icktimani slain by Sang Sapurba's champion (Malay Annals)
variants.summary: The same serpent-name as the Menangcabow ravager, cut in three by the sword Chora Samanda Kian, which carries away 190 notches; the foundation of the Pagaruyung line.

variants.name: Comparative dismembered-primordial-being myths
variants.summary: World formed from a slain primordial body; the Malay version uniquely makes the body's tears and sweat into weather.

Gabriel did so, and the serpent brake asunder, the head and forepart shooting up above the heavens, and the tail part penetrating downwards beneath the earth.

title.en: The Earth on the Buffalo's Horns

region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（採錄宇宙觀）

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, shape of the earth

summary.en: The earth is carried by a colossal buffalo standing on an island in the nether ocean. When one horn begins to tire, the buffalo tosses the world up and catches it on the other horn — and that is an earthquake. Around everything girts an immense serpent or dragon, the Ular Naga, which feeds upon its own tail.
summary.zh: 大地由巨牛負於牛角之尖，立於下界大洋中之島上。一角疲倦時，巨牛便將世界拋起、接於另一角尖——此即地震。宇宙外環巨蛇（烏拉·那伽），自噬其尾。

sensitivity.note: World-buffalo cosmology; Skeat compares the Indian elephant variant (Ramayana, Vishnu's boar).

passages.text: A further development of the Malay theory of the earth declares it to be carried by a colossal buffalo upon the tip of its horns. When one horn begins to tire the buffalo tosses it up and catches it upon the tip of the other, thus causing periodical earthquakes. This world-buffalo stands upon an island in the midst of the nether ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: The universe is girt round by an immense serpent or dragon (Ular Naga), which feeds upon its own tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: The Pauh Janggi: The Tree in Mid-Ocean That Swallows the Tides
title.zh: 寶塢江宜：吞潮之海中神樹

region.en: Middle of the great ocean (symbolic pin, Malay cosmology)
region.zh: 大洋之中（象徵性定位，馬來宇宙觀）

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, the theory of the tides

summary.en: In the middle of the great ocean grows the immense tree Pauh Janggi, at whose root a monstrous crab alternately opens and shuts the door of the sea-passage: when it opens, the waters pour out (ebb-tide); when it shuts, they back up (flood-tide). Skeat identifies the tree with the legendary palm of the coco-de-mer, whose twin nuts Malay sailors washed ashore on Sumatran coasts from a palm growing below the sea.
summary.zh: 大洋之中生巨樹『寶塢江宜』；樹根處巨蟹開合海底通道之門：門開水瀉（退潮），門閉水壅（漲潮）。斯凱特指其即雙椰子傳說之海底棕櫚——馬來水手偶於蘇門答臘海濱拾得沖上之雙椰。

sensitivity.note: Tide-myth; the tree-of-the-ocean motif parallels Indian and Oceanic world-trees.

passages.text: In the middle of the great ocean grows an immense tree, called Pauh Jangi, at the root of which a monstrous crab opens and shuts the door of the sea-passage, letting out and holding in the waters — the Malay explanation of the tides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: The tree appears to be a tradition of the Cocos Maldiva: the old belief was that the fruit was produced on a palm growing below the sea, whose fronds, according to Malay seamen, were sometimes seen in quiet bights on the Sumatran coast, and whose curious twin nuts were cast up on the shores of the Indian Ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I (with Skeat's note on the coco-de-mer); not verbatim.

title.en: The Heart of the Earth: Azrael and the Making of Adam
title.zh: 大地之心：亞茲拉爾取土造亞當

region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（符咒書神話）

texts.period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II 'Creation of Man', the Heart of the Earth

summary.en: God sends Gabriel, then Israfel, then Michael to fetch 'the Heart of the Earth' — and the Earth refuses each in turn: 'if you take away my Heart I shall assuredly die.' Only Azrael wrests it, seizing the Earth's middle finger (which stretches and becomes the jari bantu, the Devil's Finger). Gabriel mixes the white heart-clay with water — too soft; with fire — too hard; strikes out the image of Adam, and craves life for it from God.
summary.zh: 神先遣迦伯列、伊斯拉斐爾、米迦勒取『大地之心』——地神逐一拒之：『若取我心，我必死。』唯亞茲拉爾奪得，緊握地神中指（手指拉長，即『魔鬼指』）。迦伯列以白心之土和黏：加水則軟，加火則硬——終打成亞當之像，向神求其生命。

sensitivity.note: Malay modification of Arabic Adam-creation lore, as Skeat notes; treated as folk theology with care.

narrative.en:
Skeat's chapter on the creation of man records, from a Selangor charm-book dictated by a Malay magician, the fullest Malay folk version of the moulding of Adam — a local transformation of Arabic lore that keeps the Earth herself as a speaking character.

BEGINNING: THE REFUSALS. God Almighty spake unto Gabriel, 'Be not disobedient, O Gabriel, but go and get me the Heart of the Earth.' Gabriel cannot get it: 'I will not give it,' said the Earth. The Prophet Israfel goes and cannot get it; Michael goes and cannot get it. In the fuller parallel account, Azrael first salutes the Earth in orthodox fashion and is met with the same point-blank refusal, 'forasmuch as I was so created by God Almighty, and if you take away my Heart I shall assuredly die.'

MIDDLE: THE WRESTLING. Azrael loses his temper, gives the Earth a push with his right hand and his left, grasps at the Heart of the Earth and carries it back to the presence of God. The magician who dictated the account added that when Azrael stretched forth his hand, the Earth-spirit caught hold of his middle finger, which yielded to the strain, became longer than the rest, and received its Malay name of the 'Devil's Finger' (jari bantu) — an etiology of the longest finger carried inside a creation myth.

END: THE MOULDING. Gabriel takes the lump of earth which was the Earth's Heart and mixes it first with water to soften it — too soft; then with fire to harden it; and when the image is made, obtains life from God to put into it. The image of Adam is struck out, life is craved and given — and the sequel (recorded in the companion record) tells of the first image's breaking, the steel spine of Khorassan, and the descent of our Lady Eve at dawn.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) grounds the creation-of-man motif in a living Earth that must be despoiled — a price-of-life theology; (2) etiologizes the human hand (the Devil's Finger); (3) registers Malay syncretism: Qur'anic angels and Arabic traditions retold in the idiom of the Malay Earth-spirit; and (4) supplies the Malay comparative analogue to the world's clay-humans cluster (Nüwa, Enki and Ninhursag, the Maya failures, Obatala). The charm's casting of the Earth as a speaking, refusing, grieving person is its most distinctive feature and deserves emphasis: where most clay-human myths simply take the mud, the Malay magician's Earth negotiates, objects on the ground that she was made by God and will die if her heart is removed, and leaves a mark on the thief's hand. The result is a theology in which the material of human life is acknowledged to be stolen — an ethic of apology built into the first page of the human story. The second account's detail that the Heart of the Earth was white carries its own symbolism, for white is the royal colour of the Malay world; the first man is moulded, in effect, of royal clay. The charm ends in marriage and in twins: Eve descends while Adam prays, is caught, lost, and caught again, and the first children are born in pairs — handsome with handsome, plain with plain — the charm-book's quiet answer to the question of how difference entered the world.
narrative.zh: 斯凱特自雪蘭莪巫師口授之符咒書中錄得最完整的馬來造亞當傳說：神遣天使取『大地之心』，地神連拒三位天使，並言：『若取我心，我必死』；唯亞茲拉爾強奪，地神反握其手，致中指拉長成『魔鬼指』。迦伯列以心土和黏塑亞當——加水則軟、加火則硬——終成其像而求神賦生。功能：以活的地神受剝為生命之代價、釋人手指之由來、登錄馬來宗教融合、並成泥人造人跨文化母題之馬來版本（可比女媧、恩基、馬雅失敗泥人、約魯巴奧巴塔拉）。

functions: Price-of-life theology: man is moulded from the living Earth's stolen heart
Etiology of the jari bantu (the elongated middle finger) inside the creation narrative
Register of Malay-Islamic syncretism: Qur'anic angels in an animist Earth-spirit idiom
Malay analogue in the world-wide clay-humans motif cluster

title.en: The Broken Image and the Steel Spine of Khorassan

region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（符咒書神話）

texts.period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, the making and breaking of Adam's image

summary.en: When the image of Adam is raised and life craved for it, God gives life — 'Then sneezed God Almighty, and the image of Adam brake in pieces.' Azrael returns to remake it, and this time God commands that steel of Khorassan be driven down the first man's back, becoming his thirty-three bones, harder at the top, softer below — 'the harder steel shot up skywards, and the softer steel penetrated earthwards.' Thus Adam lives, in a body half mineral, half divine.
summary.zh: 亞當之像既立，求神賦生；神施生——『忽聞神打噴嚏，亞當之像碎裂』。亞茲拉爾重塑之，神命以呼羅珊之鋼打入其背，化為三十三骨——上硬下軟：『硬鋼上指諸天，軟鋼下貫大地』。亞當遂活，其身半屬礦物、半屬神造。

sensitivity.note: Sequel of the Adam-moulding charm; a Malay folk anatomy of the spine.

passages.text: Then he raised up the image of Adam, and craved Life for it from Almighty God, and God Almighty gave it Life. Then sneezed God Almighty, and the image of Adam brake in pieces, and he (Azrael) returned to remake the image of Adam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then God Almighty commanded to take steel of Khorassan, and drive it down his back, so that it became the thirty-three bones, the harder steel at the top, the softer below it. The harder steel shot up skywards, and the softer steel penetrated earthwards. Thus the image of Adam had life, and dwelt in Paradise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Tan Puteh, the Daughter of the River

region.en: Palembang river-mouth tradition (Malay legend recorded in Skeat)
region.zh: 巴鄰旁河口傳說（斯凱特採錄馬來傳說）

texts.period: Legend recorded 1890s (J.R.A.S., S.B., No. 9); published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, the legend of the foam island (Teh Purba)

summary.en: Volumes of foam collect in the river 'the size of an elephant'; a childless couple — the wife of white Semang blood — go to bathe, push aside the froth-island, and find a female infant sitting in its midst enveloped in cloud-like foam. They adopt her as 'the daughter of the river' and name her Tan Puteh (Teh Purba); as she grows, their wealth increases and the village becomes an important place — the white royal blood of the river-born child blessing the town.
summary.zh: 河面聚起大象般之泡沫堆；無子的白膚塞芒血統夫婦沐浴時推開泡沫之島，見泡沫雲團中坐一女嬰。二人收為養女，昭告鄉里，稱之『河之女』，名譚普特（德·普爾巴）；自此家道日隆，村邑漸成重鎮——河生兒之王室白血為地方賜福。

sensitivity.note: Parallel to the Annals' Putri Tunjong Bui (foam-bell princess of Palembang) — Skeat notes the kinship; flagged as a shared Malay river-foundling motif.

passages.text: Volumes of foam collected in a mass the size of an elephant. Nakhodah Kasim's wife went to bathe, and finding this island of froth in her way she attempted to move it away with a stick; she removed the upper portion of it and disclosed a female infant sitting in the midst of it enveloped all round with cloud-like foam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: The couple adopted the child willingly, for they had no children, and treated her thenceforward as their own. They assembled the villagers and gave them a feast, solemnly announcing their adoption of the daughter of the river. The child was called Tan Puteh, but her father gave her the name of Teh Purba; as she grew up the wealth of her foster-parents increased, and the village gradually became an important place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Regalia Born of Themselves at the Burning Mountain

region.en: Between the two peaks of Gunung Merapi, Menangkabau, Sumatra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保瑪拉皮雙峰之間（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Informant statement recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, magic powers of the regalia

summary.en: Skeat's Selangor informant declared that the royal regalia 'came into existence of themselves (terjadi sendiri), at a spot between the two peaks of a burning mountain (gunong merapi) in the country of Menangkabau in Sumatra'; that 'rain could not rot them nor sun blister them'; that any one who brushed past them would fall to the ground — and that no fewer than seven buffaloes must be slaughtered before the 'Moving Mountains' (two peaked state pillows) can be replaced when worn out.
summary.zh: 斯凱特之雪蘭莪消息人言：王室重器『自生』（terjadi sendiri）於蘇門答臘米南加保瑪拉皮烈火雙峰之間；『雨不能朽之，日不能灼之』；凡人掠其身而過者立仆；若『移山』（一對尖形王枕）用舊需換，須先宰水牛七頭。

sensitivity.note: Regalia-sanctity belief; living royal-institution lore, paraphrased respectfully.

passages.text: My informant declared that these objects came into existence of themselves (terjadi sendiri), at a spot between the two peaks of a burning mountain (gunong merapi) in the country of Menangkabau in Sumatra. He also averred that 'rain could not rot them nor sun blister them,' and that any one who brushed past them would fall to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: No fewer than seven buffaloes have to be slaughtered before the 'moving mountains' (when worn out) can be replaced — the peaked state pillows of the royal couch, among the least conspicuous but most carefully hedged objects of the regalia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sultan Whose One Eye Is the Sun: The Title-List of Menangcabow
title.zh: 一目如日之蘇丹：米南加保王號全錄

region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保巴加爾容

texts.period: Recorded by Marsden 1784 (History of Sumatra, p. 270); reproduced in Skeat 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, reproducing Marsden's enumeration of the Sultan of Menangcabow's titles

summary.en: Marsden recorded the full pretensions of the Sultan of Menangcabow: son of Raja Iscunder-sulcarnainny; master of the sword Chooree-se-mendong-geree with its hundred and ninety gaps 'made in the conflict with the arch-devil Se Cattee-moono, whom it slew'; master of fresh water in the ocean to the extent of a day's sailing; of the cock Sengonannee, unconquered; of the buffalo Se Binnooang Satiee whose horns are ten feet asunder; of the gun brought from heaven; 'who may slay at pleasure without being guilty of a crime'; and of whom 'one of whose eyes is as the sun and the other as the moon.'
summary.zh: 馬爾斯登錄得米南加保蘇丹全銜：亞歷山德羅之裔；佩劍『珠里色門東』上有百九十缺口——『誅滅大魔西卡提穆納』之戰所留；掌大洋一日航程內之淡水；畜不敗之雄雞森戈南尼；畜水牛西賓努安薩蒂，雙角相距十尺；有天降之銃；『可任意殺人而不為罪』；『一目如日、一目如月』。

sensitivity.note: Royal title-catalogue; the 190-notch sword directly cross-links to the Sacatimuna serpent slain in the Annals and the serpent killed by Gabriel in Skeat's charm-books.

passages.text: The Sultan of Menangcabow, whose residence is at Pagarooyoong, who is king of kings, son of Raja Iscunder-sulcarnainny — possessed of the sword named Chooree-se-mendong-geree, which has an hundred and ninety gaps, made in the conflict with the arch-devil Se Cattee-moono, whom it slew; who is master of fresh water in the ocean, to the extent of a day's sailing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784), p. 270, reproduced in Skeat (1900); not verbatim.

passages.text: He is possessed of the buffalo named Se Binnooang Satiee, whose horns are ten feet asunder; of the unconquered cock Sengonannee; of a gun brought from heaven; who may slay at pleasure without being guilty of a crime; who, when he goes to sleep, wakes not till the gandang nobat sounds; one of whose eyes is as the sun and the other as the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784), p. 270, reproduced in Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
